ca-a-igloo.s: An igloo is a house made of snow bricks. The Inuit, a people of the north, cut thick blocks of snow and lay them in a circle, and each new row leans a little closer to the middle. It makes a spiral, and at the end a round roof, a dome. The gaps are filled with snow. Snow is full of air, and air keeps the warmth in. So inside an igloo, even in a hard frost, it is much warmer than outside. Long ago, hunters could build one in a couple of hours when they needed a place to sleep on a journey.

ca-a-inuksuk.s: In the northern tundra, where there are no trees and no fences, you suddenly see a little man made of stones. It is an inuksuk. It is built from big stones: legs, a body, and sometimes arms. The word means something like “standing in for a person”. Inuksuit show travellers the way, tell them where the good fishing places are, and help hunters. If you see one, it means people have been here before. A stone man like this was also drawn on the badge of the 2010 Winter Olympic Games.

ca-a-parka.s: The whole world knows the word “parka”, but it was the northern peoples who invented this kind of coat. Long ago, parkas were sewn from caribou skins: a caribou’s fur is hollow inside and keeps in the warmth better than many cloths. Inuit mums had a special parka called an amauti. It has a big hood at the back where the baby sat. It is as warm as a little nest in there, and Mum’s hands are free. Needles were made from bones and thread from sinews. The sewing was beautiful, with patterns.
a: In a pocket on the sleeve

ca-a-narwhal.s: In the cold waters of the Arctic lives the narwhal, a kind of whale. It has a long twisted tusk sticking out, like the unicorn in fairy tales. In fact it is a tooth, and it grows right out of the upper jaw, most often on the left. It can be up to three metres long. Long ago, people thought such tusks came from magic animals, and they sold them as unicorn horns. Narwhals live in groups, love the cold and dive very deep. Their skin is spotted, grey and white.

ca-b-rideau.s: In Canada’s capital, Ottawa, there is a canal called the Rideau Canal. In summer, boats sail on it, but in winter the water freezes and the canal turns into a huge skating rink! It stretches for almost eight kilometres. People skate to work and to school, and then drink hot chocolate at stalls right on the ice. According to the Guinness Book of Records, it is the biggest natural ice rink in the world, because the winter itself freezes the ice.
a: It freezes and becomes a skating rink
It goes off to warm countries
It fills up with hot cocoa

ca-b-orcas.s: Not far from Vancouver, orcas live in the sea. They are not fish, they are big dolphins! Orcas swim in families, and the boss of a family is usually the grandmother. The babies stay close to their mum for many years. The families talk to each other with clicks and whistles, and each one has its own “accent”. People go out in boats to watch orcas, but they do not go close, so as not to scare them. And if it is raining in Vancouver, which it often is, people simply put on their raincoats.
a: A seagull sitting on its back

ca-b-fundy.s: The Bay of Fundy in eastern Canada has the highest tides in the world. Twice a day the sea rises and falls, and at the biggest tides the water changes by as much as sixteen metres. That is like a five-storey house! At low tide, boats lie right on the bottom, on the wet sand, and you can walk on the seabed. Then the water comes back, and the boats float again. In one tide, billions of tonnes of water flow into the bay.
a: They lie on the bottom, on the sand
They fly off into the clouds

ca-b-banff-bridges.s: In Banff National Park, in the Rocky Mountains, bridges and tunnels were built across a big road, but not for people, for animals. There are six bridges and thirty-eight tunnels. The bridges are covered in grass and trees, so they look like woodland clearings. Deer, mountain sheep and even grizzly bears cross over them. This way the animals go wherever they like, and the cars drive along calmly without scaring anyone.

ca-b-naismith.s: Basketball was invented by a Canadian, James Naismith. In 1891 he worked as a PE teacher in the USA. In winter the boys were bored in the gym, and he needed a new game. He hung two peach baskets on the balcony, took a football and wrote thirteen rules. The baskets hung about three metres high, and today the hoop in basketball hangs at the same height.

ca-b-poutine.s: In Quebec, people invented a dish with a funny name: poutine (say “poo-TEEN”). It is hot chips, with pieces of fresh young cheese on top, and then it is all covered with warm gravy. The cheese in poutine is special: while it is fresh, it squeaks on your teeth! The dish began in the villages of Quebec, and now it is eaten all over Canada. Grown-ups say poutine is best when it is cold outside.

cas-b-delfiny.s: Boats set off from Cascais to look for dolphins. The dolphins live in the ocean not far from the shore. They love to swim right beside the front of a boat, jumping out of the water. Every dolphin has its own special whistle, a bit like our names. When friends hear it, they know who is calling. You do not see dolphins every day, so everyone on the boat watches the waves and waits for a grey back to flash by.
a: By the smell of a tail

cas-b-osminog.s: Octopuses hide among the rocks along the coast of Portugal. They have eight arms and three whole hearts! Two send blood to the gills, and one sends it round the whole body. An octopus has bluish blood. It is very clever: it can open jars, find its way, and change colour to blend in with the stones. In the day it usually rests in its little den, and it comes out to catch crabs when it starts to get dark on the shore.

cas-c-cork.s: Cork is the bark of a special oak tree, the cork oak. Once every nine years, skilled workers carefully cut off the bark with small axes. The tree does not get ill, and it grows new bark. Cork is used for more than bottle stoppers: bags, purses, hats and even shoes are made from it. In the shops of Portugal, including in Cascais, you can touch light, warm cork and feel how soft it is.

cas-comboio.s: A train runs from Cascais to Lisbon, and almost all the way it goes beside the ocean. From the window you can see waves, beaches, old forts and fishing boats. The railway to Cascais opened in 1889. Then people from Lisbon began to take the train to the seaside to swim and to walk. Later, some of the first electric trains in Portugal ran here.

cas-cresmina.s: Next to Guincho beach lies the Cresmina dune, a big hill of sand. But this hill does not stay still! The strong wind blows and blows, and carries the sand grain by grain. In one year the dune moves about the length of a bus. To keep from stepping on the plants, people walk on wooden paths. From there you can see the wind drawing little waves in the sand.

cas-lota.s: When the fishermen of Cascais come back from the sea, they bring their catch to the lota. The lota is a fish auction, where fish is sold by special rules. The boxes of fish are shown one by one. First the price is high, and then it gets lower and lower. The buyer who gives a sign first takes the box. This way fresh fish quickly gets to the shops and restaurants.
a: It flies up to the moon
It jumps back into the sea

cas-fleming.s: In Estoril, next to Cascais, there is a casino. It is a big, fancy building where grown-ups play cards and other games. In front of it is a garden with palm trees. A long time ago, the English writer Ian Fleming stayed in Estoril and watched people play in the casino. They say the Estoril casino helped him to think up the first book about the brave spy James Bond. A spy is a secret agent, and many films were made about James Bond later.

cas-b-sardina-na-hlebe.s: In summer, the seaside in Portugal smells of smoke, because sardines are grilled over hot coals. They do not need a plate. The hot little fish is laid right on a slice of bread. The bread soaks up the juice and becomes the tastiest bit. Sardines live in big shoals and swim shoulder to shoulder, as if they were marching. The fishermen of Cascais catch them in nets, and then they grill them on the shore for everyone.

cas-b-olushi.s: In winter, big white birds with black wing tips fly over the ocean near Portugal. They are gannets. When a gannet spots a fish, it folds its wings and drops like an arrow, from as high as a tall block of flats. It hits the water as fast as a car on a motorway. So that its head does not hurt, it has little air cushions under its skin. Then the gannet pops up with a fish in its beak.
a: It drops into the water like an arrow
It digs with its feet in the sand

cas-b-kajtsurf.s: Guincho beach, not far from Cascais, is loved by everyone who needs wind. In the sky above the waves float huge, bright kites, striped, green and yellow. Under each one stands a person on a board, a kitesurfer. The wind fills the kite and pulls it forward, and the board along the water with it. The kitesurfer can even jump over the waves like a grasshopper. The whole beach looks up and laughs with joy.

cas-c-santini-ice-cream.s: In 1949, an Italian man called Attilio Santini opened a little ice cream shop on Tamariz beach, near Cascais. Later, another shop like it opened in Cascais itself. People liked the ice cream so much that on hot days there is a queue at the counter. The family says they still make it from the same recipes as many years ago. And there are so many flavours that your eyes go wide: chocolate, berries, lemon.

cas-b-luzhi-na-kamnyah.s: When the ocean goes out, little pools are left between the rocks. For a crab, it is a whole home! Take a look into one. Sea anemones that look like flowers sit there, a starfish creeps along, and tiny fish dart about. They are all waiting for the water to come back. Look at them gently, do not pull them out, and put the stones back, because under them is somebody’s bedroom. The best time to hunt for wonders is just after the tide goes out.

cas-c-calceteiro.s: The pavements of Cascais are laid by hand. The pavement maker crouches down with a little hammer and picks up small stones: white ones of limestone and black ones of basalt. He sets them into the sand one by one and taps them until each stone sits flat. This is how patterns appear in the squares: waves, fish, ships and stars. The work is slow, but you can walk on these pictures as much as you like.

chn-a-stena-gory.s: The Great Wall of China does not lie in a straight line. It climbs over the mountain ridges like a long stone ribbon. Up, down and up again. In some places the steps are so steep that you have to hold the rail. The Wall was built of brick and stone, and in lands with no trees even of packed earth. Add up all its parts, ditches and natural barriers, and it is more than twenty thousand kilometres long. That is about halfway round the whole Earth!

chn-a-zapgorod-koshki.s: The Forbidden City is a museum now, and cats live there. Ginger, grey and patchy ones. People say there are more than a hundred and fifty. The museum workers call them guards: the cats catch mice that could nibble the old things. In the daytime the cats hide from the crowds, and they walk about mostly at night. The cats are looked after. They are fed and given medicine when they are ill.
a: They guard the gates from lions

chn-a-panda-malysh.s: A newborn panda is tiny and pink, with almost no fur. It weighs about a hundred grams, like a bar of chocolate. Its mum is hundreds of times heavier. For about a month the baby cannot see, because its eyes are closed. Mum holds it gently in her paw. But the baby grows fast, gets black and white fur and soon begins to crawl.
a: About as much as a chocolate bar
About as much as a big watermelon
About as much as a brick

chn-a-army-lica.s: Underground near the city of Xi’an stand thousands of clay soldiers. They are as tall as a person, or even taller. The makers shaped their faces, and almost no two are the same. One has a moustache, another a beard, a third a different hairstyle. Some soldiers look serious, and others seem to smile a little. Visitors walk along the rows and look for the kindest face.
a: Almost no two are the same

chn-a-shelk-tut.s: Silk is made by the silkworm caterpillar. It hatches from a tiny egg, very small. It eats only mulberry leaves, day after day. People say that when there are many caterpillars, their munching sounds like rain on leaves. In a month it grows dozens of times heavier and changes its skin four times. That is why people in China grew mulberry trees right next to the silk.

chn-b-newyear-envelope.s: At New Year in China, children are given red envelopes. Inside there is money, and kind words are printed on the envelope. The envelope is called a hongbao. Grown-up relatives give it and wish: grow big and healthy. You take the gift with both hands, as if it were something fragile, and politely say “thank you”. Usually you do not open the envelope in front of everyone.

chn-b-dragon-dance.s: At festivals a long dragon “crawls” along the streets of China. It is made of cloth and paper, and inside it, like in a train carriage, dozens of people walk. Each one holds a pole and lifts their own piece of the body. In front runs a person with a ball, like a pearl. The dragon plays and chases it. When everyone steps together, the dragon wiggles as if it were alive.

chn-b-guilin-cormorants.s: On the Li River you can sometimes see a fisherman on a long bamboo raft. Black birds called cormorants sit beside him. The bird dives and catches a fish, and the fisherman takes it. A thin little ring is put round the bird’s neck, so that it cannot swallow a big fish. The cormorant eats the small fish itself. This is a very old way of fishing: birds and people work together.

chn-b-tea-legend.s: An old legend tells of a ruler called Shennong. He liked to drink only boiled water. One day he sat under a tree while the water was boiling. The wind blew off a few little leaves, and they fell into the pot. The water turned golden and smelled lovely. The ruler took a sip and was surprised: the drink was pleasant and made him feel lively. That is how, says the legend, people found tea, a very long time ago.

chn-b-zodiac.s: In the Chinese calendar every year has its own animal. There are twelve: rat, ox, tiger, rabbit, dragon, snake, horse, goat, monkey, rooster, dog and pig. An old tale says they held a race across a river, and in one version it went like this. The clever rat climbed onto the ox’s back, jumped off at the finish and came first. That is why the year of the rat counts as the first. After twelve years the circle starts again.

chn-a-pekin-gnezdo.s: There is a stadium in Beijing that looks like a giant bird’s nest. It was built for the 2008 Olympic Games. The steel beams are woven together like twigs, and you can see the sky between them. From far away, it looks as if giant birds have built a nest. Tens of thousands of people can sit inside. No wonder it is called “the Bird’s Nest”.

chn-b-chopsticks-three-thousand.s: People in China have eaten with chopsticks for about three thousand years. At first, they say, chopsticks were used for cooking, to lift food out of a hot pot. Later they came to the table. They are made of bamboo or wood. Instead of a fork and knife, you hold two thin sticks. With some practice, you can pick up rice, noodles and even a tiny pea.

chn-b-lantern-festival.s: The New Year celebrations in China end with the Lantern Festival. It is on the fifteenth day of the new year. In the evening, the streets and parks glow with thousands of lanterns. They come in the shapes of fish, rabbits and dragons. Some lanterns have riddles written on them, and everyone wants to solve them. On this day people also eat sweet balls made of rice flour. They are called yuanxiao.

chn-b-shanghai-maglev.s: In Shanghai there is a train that does not touch the rails. It floats above the track on an invisible magnetic cushion. That is why it runs so smoothly and quietly. It used to speed up to almost 430 kilometres an hour, and today it goes a little slower. It travels the thirty kilometres to the airport in only eight minutes. Passengers barely have time to look at the city outside!

chn-b-terraces-yuanyang.s: In the south of China, the mountains look like giant staircases. These are the Yuanyang rice terraces. People carved the steps into the hillsides many hundreds of years ago. In spring the steps are filled with water, and each one shines like a mirror. The sky and the clouds are reflected in the water. Early in the morning, when there is mist over the mountains, it looks as if the staircase goes right up into the sky.

chn-b-noodles.s: On their birthday, people in China eat long noodles. They are called longevity noodles. One strand is made very long, and you try not to bite it through but to eat it whole. People say that the longer the noodle, the longer the life. It is just a fun and kind good-luck wish, and a tasty one. So on the party table the noodles are served uncut and long, and everyone wishes the birthday child good health.

chn-b-compass.s: People say that about two thousand years ago, the first thing like a compass was invented in China. It was described as a spoon made of a special stone, a magnet. It was placed on a smooth board, and it turned its handle to the south. Later came a needle that floated on water or hung on a thread. Sailors took it with them on voyages. That way the needle helped them not to get lost on the open sea.

chn-b-two-rivers.s: China has two very famous rivers. The Yangtze is the longest in Asia, more than six thousand kilometres. It flows through mountains and plains and runs into the sea near Shanghai. The Yellow River, in Chinese Huang He, is also very long. Its water is yellow because it carries a lot of sand and clay. Both rivers flow from west to east, and people have lived on their banks since ancient times.
a: It carries a lot of sand and clay

chn-a-bumaga-vyrezki.s: In China, people can cut real pictures out of paper. They take a red sheet, fold it in half or in four, and cut it with scissors. Unfold it, and a pattern appears: a flower, a fish, a little bird. The two halves are the same because the paper was folded. These paper cuttings are stuck on windows, and the light shines prettily through the red flowers.
a: The paper is folded in half
The pattern is drawn with a ruler
The paper is painted on both sides

chn-b-hieroglyph-pictures.s: A very long time ago, Chinese characters were just tiny pictures. A mountain was drawn with three sharp peaks. The sun was a little circle with a dot in the middle. A tree was drawn with a trunk, branches and roots. Over time the pictures became simpler and turned into strokes. But if you look closely, you can still see three peaks in the character for “mountain”!

es-holiday-grapes.s: On New Year’s Eve, people in Spain eat grapes. When the clock strikes twelve, you must eat twelve grapes, one for every bong. That is not easy, because you have to chew very fast! Each grape is said to bring good luck for one month of the new year. So before the party, shops sell grapes in little tins: twelve in each.

es-holiday-kings.s: In Spain, children get their presents from the Three Kings: Melchior, Caspar and Balthazar. On the evening of the fifth of January there is a parade, and the kings throw sweets into the crowd. Children leave their shoes by the door and put out water for the kings’ camels. On the morning of the sixth there are presents next to the shoes! With tea, people eat a round cake with a surprise inside: whoever finds the little king gets to wear a paper crown.

es-animals-lynx.s: In the south of Spain lives the Iberian lynx. It is a wild cat with a spotty coat, a short tail and little tassels on its ears, and fluffy whiskers on both sides of its face. It loves rabbits best of all. Not long ago there were very few of these lynxes left, but people started looking after them, and now there are more again. It is hard to spot one: the lynx is shy and likes to hide in the bushes.

es-food-churros.s: In Spain, people love churros for breakfast or a snack. They are long, golden sticks of dough fried in oil. You dip them in thick, warm chocolate, so thick that a spoon almost stands up in it. Churros are crunchy outside and soft inside. They are sold in little cafés, and sometimes at fairs, and children go home with chocolate moustaches.

es-segovia-aqueduct.s: In the middle of the streets of Segovia stands a Roman aqueduct. It was built almost two thousand years ago to bring water from the mountains to the town. It is about twenty-eight metres high and has more than a hundred and sixty arches. The most amazing thing is that the heavy granite stones sit on top of each other with no mortar or glue. Only their own weight holds them. And the aqueduct is still standing, strong and beautiful.
a: Only the weight of the stones

es-altamira-bison.s: In the north of Spain, in the Altamira cave, there are bison painted on the ceiling. They were painted by people in the Stone Age, a very, very long time ago, maybe more than fifteen thousand years ago. The artists used red and black paint and used the bumps in the rock, so the bison look round and solid. The paintings were first noticed by a little girl, the daughter of a man who was exploring the cave. Today an exact copy has been made next to it, so the real paintings are not spoiled.

es-bilbao-puppy.s: In front of the museum in Bilbao sits a giant puppy called Puppy. He is as tall as a four-storey house, about twelve metres. But the most amazing thing is that his “fur” is made of living flowers! Gardeners plant tens of thousands of plants in a metal frame, and inside are hidden pipes that water the puppy. In spring and summer he is bright and colourful, and every now and then the flowers are changed.

es-mallorca-cave.s: On the island of Majorca there are the Drach caves. Stone icicles grow from the ceiling and the floor: stalactites and stalagmites. And there is an underground lake hidden inside! Visitors glide across it in boats, and sometimes musicians play right on the water, and the music echoes through the cave. Lamps light up the rock, and the cave looks like a fairy-tale palace under the ground.

es-cierva-autogiro.s: A Spanish engineer called Juan de la Cierva invented a machine called the autogyro. It has a propeller at the front, like an aeroplane, and a big rotor on top. The rotor on top spins by itself, pushed by the air rushing past. The first successful flight of an autogyro was in January 1923, near Madrid, in a place called Getafe. Cierva’s invention later helped scientists to make helicopters.
a: A big rotor, turned by the air

es-cuenca-houses.s: In the town of Cuenca there are houses that seem to hang in the air. They were built many centuries ago at the edge of a cliff, and their wooden balconies stick out right over the deep gorge of the Huécar river. That is why they are called the hanging houses. From below they look like a picture from a fairy tale, and from above you can see mountains and forests. Today one of the houses is a museum with paintings by modern artists.
a: Their balconies hang over the gorge

de-knut.s: In December 2006, a little polar bear called Knut was born in Berlin Zoo. His mother did not feed him, so a keeper called Thomas took care of him. He fed him milk from a bottle and looked after him day and night. Knut grew into a fluffy, playful bear, and people all over the world heard about him. They came to the zoo from many countries just to see him.

de-hamburg-wunderland.s: In Hamburg there is Miniatur Wunderland, the biggest model railway in the world. It has tiny towns, mountains and rivers, and hundreds of trains drive through them. There is even a tiny airport: the little planes roll onto the runway all by themselves and take off! The windows of the little houses glow, and every now and then night falls, and lights come on in all the towns. There are so many little people that you cannot count them all.

de-munich-glockenspiel.s: On the main square of Munich, Marienplatz, there is a clock on the town hall tower with figures that come to life. Every day at eleven and at noon, forty-three bells ring, and life-size figures ride out and spin around: knights fight in a tournament, and coopers, who are people who make barrels, dance their dance. At the very end, a golden cockerel crows at the top. People gather early and look up.

de-gutenberg.s: Long, long ago, books were copied out by hand, and one book took months. Then, in the German city of Mainz, a craftsman called Johannes Gutenberg had an idea: to print books with metal letters. Each letter was cast in metal. The letters were put together into words and lines, covered with ink and pressed onto paper, like a stamp. So one page could be printed again and again. There were more books, and many more people learned to read. That was more than five hundred years ago.
a: Paper ones, as light as clouds

de-f-haribo.s: The name Haribo is a secret code. A confectioner called Hans Riegel lived in the city of Bonn, and in 1920 he opened a sweet factory there. He took the first two letters of his first name, of his surname and the name of his city: HAns, RIegel, BOnn. That makes HARIBO. Two years later he made the first gummy bears. They were called “dancing bears”, because at that time fairs often had real dancing bears.
a: From the maker’s name and his city

de-f-shultyute.s: In Germany, on the first day of school, children are given a huge paper cone called a Schultüte. It can be almost as tall as the child. Parents fill it with sweets, pencils, rubbers and little toys. This tradition is about two hundred years old. An old story says that in the teacher’s cellar there is a tree on which these cones ripen. When they are ripe, it is time to start learning.
a: A big cone full of sweets

de-f-shvebebahn.s: In the city of Wuppertal, a train runs through the air. It is called the Schwebebahn. The carriages hang from a rail high above the river Wupper, and boats float underneath. It opened in 1901 and still runs today. In 1950 a circus had a funny idea and put a baby elephant called Tuffi in a carriage. She got scared by the noise, jumped out of the window into the river and swam away. Tuffi climbed onto the bank with just a few scratches and lived for a long time.
a: Hanging above a river in Wuppertal

de-n-watt.s: On the shores of the North Sea, the water goes out very, very far twice a day. This is called low tide. What is left is the wet sea floor, called the Wattenmeer, and you can walk on it in wellies. Under your feet there is sand, shells and tiny worms, and seals lie on the sandbanks. Then the water comes back, and that is high tide. So people only walk on the sea floor with a grown-up guide who knows when the tide comes in.
a: The tide goes out and comes in

de-p-rentgen.s: One evening, a scientist called Wilhelm Röntgen noticed in a dark room that a screen was glowing, although there was no light nearby. So there must be invisible rays! He did not know what they were, so he called them “X-rays”. Then he took the first picture: his wife’s hand with a ring on it, and you could see the little bones. Today doctors take pictures like this, and in Germany they are still called Röntgen pictures.

de-f-ampelmann.s: In Berlin, a little man in a hat stands on the traffic lights. His name is Ampelmann. He was invented in 1961 by a traffic psychologist called Karl Peglau, because it is easier for children to understand a little man than just a coloured circle. When Berlin became one city again, people wanted to replace him with an ordinary one. But Berliners loved him so much that he stayed. Now he is on T-shirts, mugs and sweets. In some cities, little traffic-light girls with plaits have appeared too.
a: A little man in a hat on a traffic light

ind-a-taj-tsvet.s: In the Indian city of Agra stands the Taj Mahal, a palace-tomb. It is made entirely of white marble. Early in the morning it looks soft pink. In the daytime it shines white, and towards evening it turns golden. On a moonlit night it seems to glow silver. The marble is always the same, only the light changes. That is why people come here at different hours and look at it again and again.

ind-a-slon-hobot.s: An elephant’s trunk is its nose and upper lip grown together and made very long. It has many thousands of muscles, so it is bendy and strong. An elephant can lift a thick log and pick up a tiny nut from the ground. When an elephant is thirsty, it sucks up water with its trunk and pours it into its mouth. With its trunk it sniffs, says hello to friends and cuddles its baby.
a: It sucks it up with its trunk and pours it into its mouth
It laps it with its tongue, like a cat

ind-a-tigr-polosy.s: Every tiger has its own pattern of stripes. There are no two tigers with the same pattern, just as there are no two identical fingerprints. There are stripes even on the skin under the fur. Scientists put cameras in the forest that take pictures of passing tigers. From the stripes they know each tiger and where it lives. This way they can count the tigers without bothering them.
a: By the size of its whiskers

ind-a-pavlin-hvost.s: What we call a peacock’s tail is really long feathers on its back. They can be more than a metre long. Each feather has a shiny “eye”. When a peacock wants to impress a peahen, he spreads his feathers like a fan, and slowly turns and shakes them. That is his dance. People say peacocks dance for the rain, but mostly it just happens in the rainy season. Every year after summer the feathers fall out, and then new ones grow.

ind-a-holi-kraski.s: In spring, in March, India celebrates Holi, the festival of colours. People put on old white clothes and go out into the street with little bags of coloured powder. The powder is called gulal. Everyone throws it at each other, laughing and hugging. In an hour faces and hair turn pink, yellow, blue and green. Grown-ups and children stop looking different from each other, and everyone is equally happy.

ind-a-diwali-diya.s: At Diwali people light little diya lamps. They are tiny clay bowls. Oil is poured into them, and a cotton wick is put in the oil. Potters make and bake enough bowls for a whole city. The diyas are set out in rows on window sills and by the door. The little flames shiver in the wind, but still they shine. They look like golden drops.

ind-b-chess-born.s: Chess was invented in India, a very long time ago, about fifteen hundred years, people say. The old game was called chaturanga, which means “four parts”. It had pieces for foot soldiers, horsemen, elephants and chariots. Then the game travelled along the trade roads to Persia, and from there it reached Europe. The bishop and the rook are grandchildren of the Indian elephants and chariots. Everyone who moves a pawn across the board is playing an Indian game!

ind-b-dabbawala.s: In Mumbai live people who carry lunches. They are called dabbawalas. In the morning they collect hot lunches in metal boxes from people’s homes and take them to offices by bicycle and train. After lunch the empty boxes go back home. About two hundred thousand boxes are carried like this every day! There is no address on the lid, but there are signs, numbers and colours. They show where to take the lunch. This work is more than a hundred years old.
a: Signs, numbers and colours on the box

ind-b-kerala-houseboats.s: In the state of Kerala there are quiet green canals and lakes. Houseboats float on them. They are made of wood and tied together with ropes of coconut fibre, with almost no nails. The roof is woven from palm leaves. Long ago such boats carried rice, and now travellers live on them. The boat glides slowly, palm trees sway on the banks, and for dinner there is often fish with rice.

ind-a-gang-delfin.s: A rare river dolphin lives in the Ganges. It has a long, thin nose, and its eyes see almost nothing. The river water is muddy, so seeing is not needed here. The dolphin finds its way by echo: it makes clicking sounds and listens to how they bounce off fish and riverbanks. It often swims on its side. Few of these dolphins are left, and people try to protect them.
a: By the echo of its clicks

ind-a-kaziranga.s: In the north-east of India there is a park called Kaziranga. Tall grass grows there, taller than an elephant, and there are many marshy lakes. About two thirds of all the Indian rhinos in the world live in this park. They have one horn, and their skin lies in folds like armour. Rhinos love to roll in the mud to keep cool. Macaque monkeys jump about in the trees nearby, and sometimes elephants walk along the paths.

ind-b-our-digits.s: The numbers 1, 2, 3 and the rest came to us from India. They reached Europe through Arab traders and scholars, so they are called “Arabic numerals”. Indian scholars wrote numbers so that the place of a digit shows how big it is: in 21 and in 12 the digits are the same, but the numbers are different. This made counting on paper much easier than with Roman numerals.

ind-b-yoga-animals.s: Many yoga poses are named after living things. In the cobra pose you lie on your tummy and lift your chest like a snake peeping out of the grass. In the tree pose you stand on one leg and stretch your arms up like branches. In the dog pose, like a dog stretching after sleep, you press your hands and feet into the floor and lift your back into a hill. Try it at home. It will look funny!

ind-b-sari-cloth.s: A sari is a long piece of cloth, usually five or six metres, and sometimes up to nine. The amazing thing is that it is not cut or sewn. The cloth is wrapped around the body, and the end is thrown over the shoulder. The same sari can be worn in different ways, and every region has its own folds. A sari can be cotton for a hot day or silk for a party. And the patterns on it, flowers, birds and golden edges, tell whole stories too.

ind-b-chaiwalla.s: When a train stops at a station, the chaiwallas, the tea sellers, run along the platform. They carry a kettle and shout, “Chai, chai!” They pour hot, sweet tea with milk and spices into little clay cups. When you have finished, you can smash the cup, and the clay becomes earth again. In many stations people still drink tea this way.

ind-b-bollywood-songs.s: Indian films are special: suddenly the characters start to sing and dance. They dance in meadows, in markets and on the roofs of trains. Many of these films are made in Mumbai, which used to be called Bombay. From the words “Bombay” and “Hollywood” came the funny word Bollywood. A film lasts about three hours, and there is an interval in the middle. Everyone in the country knows the songs from the films.

ind-b-mango-fruit.s: The mango is one of the most loved fruits in India, and it is the national fruit. There are hundreds of kinds: some are small like an egg, others big and heavy. One famous kind is called Alphonso, and it is very sweet and fragrant. In the hot summer the markets are full of heaps of yellow and orange fruit, and the air smells sweet. Inside a mango there is a big stone, and the flesh is juicy and makes your fingers sticky.

ind-b-jaipur-pink.s: Jaipur is a city in Rajasthan, and it is called the Pink City. The old houses there are painted a warm pink, almost like a sunset. On the main street stands the Palace of the Winds. It is a wall of windows, with almost a thousand narrow windows with carved screens. A cool breeze comes in through them. People say that women looked out at the street from there without being seen.

ind-b-cricket.s: People in India love cricket. They play not only in big stadiums, but on any street and in any yard. Instead of a goal, they put up bricks or a pile of stones, and sometimes a bat is carved from a piece of wood. The ball is a tennis ball or a ball made of rags. There are also huge stadiums that hold more than a hundred thousand people. When their favourite team plays, the whole street is glued to the television.

ind-b-mehendi.s: Henna is made from the dried leaves of a bush. The leaves are ground to a powder, water is added, and it becomes a green paste. It is squeezed from a little paper cone onto the palms and fingers to draw flowers and swirls. When the paste is dry, it is brushed off, and a reddish-brown pattern stays on the skin. It lasts one or two weeks. People draw mehendi for festivals and weddings.

isr-a-ne-tonut.s: The Dead Sea is the saltiest sea of all. Its water is about ten times saltier than the sea at home. The salty water is thick and pushes you up. You can lie on your back and float like on a mattress, even with a newspaper in your hands! But don’t splash or dive, because the salt stings your eyes. No fish can live in it, so people call it “dead”. And its shore is the lowest place on land.
a: The water is very salty and thick

isr-a-koraly-ejlat.s: Eilat sits right beside the Red Sea. The water there is warm and clear. Under the water grows a coral reef. Corals look like colourful trees, fingers and brains: red, pink and yellow. Clownfish, parrotfish and sleepy sea turtles swim between them. Reefs are very fragile, so we must not touch them. It is better to look with a mask or from a boat. Nearby there is also a bay where dolphins live free and decide for themselves when to swim up.

isr-a-ejn-gedi.s: In the hot desert by the Dead Sea hides a green oasis called Ein Gedi. Streams run there, waterfalls splash, and trees give shade. The water comes from springs, so you can cool off and rest. Nubian ibexes with big curved horns live among the rocks. They jump skilfully from stone to stone. You can also meet hyraxes, small fluffy animals a bit like marmots. They sunbathe and are not afraid of people at all.

isr-a-krater-ramon.s: In the Negev desert there is a huge stone valley. It is called Ramon Crater, or in the local language a makhtesh. It is about forty kilometres long and more than three hundred metres deep. It sounds like a hole made by a space rock, but really rain and wind slowly carved it out. The rocks in the valley are colourful: yellow, red and purple. Along the edge you can meet Nubian ibexes, who wander calmly by the cliff.
a: A space rock that fell down

isr-b-hula-cranes.s: Every autumn and spring, hundreds of millions of birds fly over Israel. It lies on the way from Europe to Africa and back. In the Hula Valley, in the north, birds can rest by the lake and in the fields. Cranes are easy to spot: more than a hundred thousand pass through, and thousands stay for the winter. They walk across the fields on long legs and trumpet loudly and beautifully. People visit the Agamon Hula park to watch them.
a: They can rest and find food

isr-b-drip-irrigation.s: Israel has many deserts and little water, so people there invented drip irrigation. Water comes out through thin pipes with tiny holes, right at the plant’s root, drop by drop. Nothing is wasted or dries up in the sun. The engineer Simcha Blass said that the idea came from a tree that grew well next to a leaky pipe. In 1965 a kibbutz called Hatzerim began making these systems, and now farmers in many countries use them.
a: Up into the sky like rain

isr-b-usb-flash.s: Have you ever seen a USB stick? It is a tiny thing where you can save photos, music and whole books, and then plug it into a computer. One of the first sticks was made in the year 2000 by a company from Israel. It was called “DiskOnKey”, which means “disk on a key”, because you could carry it on your key ring with your keys. Before that, people carried their files on big disks. Now a whole library fits in your pocket.
a: You carried it on a key ring with your keys
It was made from an iron key

isr-b-cherry-tomato.s: Small sweet tomatoes that you want to pop in your mouth whole are called cherry tomatoes, after the little round cherry fruit. They existed before, but they were delicate and burst and went bad quickly. In the 1970s, Israeli scientists and farmers grew kinds that keep longer and are easy to carry. Now cherry tomatoes sit on shop shelves in many countries. People still argue about who invented them first, but Israel certainly helped make them famous.

isr-b-hummus.s: Hummus is a favourite dish in Israel. It is made from chickpeas, which look like little golden nuts. The chickpeas are boiled and mashed into a soft purée. Then people add tahini, which is sesame paste, lemon juice and garlic, and pour a spoonful of olive oil on top. You eat hummus by dipping warm pitta bread in it. There are whole cafés that serve only hummus, and every cook is sure that his hummus is the tastiest.

isr-a-pljazh-matkot.s: The beaches of Tel Aviv stretch for many kilometres along the sea, and the sand is soft and golden. People love to play matkot here. You need two wooden bats and a small rubber ball. Two players stand apart and hit the ball back and forth, trying not to drop it. The winner is the one who keeps going the longest. The game is so simple that grandmas and children play it, and all day you can hear the tock of the ball over the sand.
a: Wooden bats and a rubber ball

isr-a-medovyj-kamen.s: Jerusalem is a city made of pale stone. The houses, walls and streets are built from limestone dug out of the nearby hills. In the daytime the stone looks almost white. At sunset it turns honey-coloured and a little pink, as if the city is lit from inside. People say it is the loveliest time for a walk. Long ago the city made a rule: new houses are covered in the same stone. So the old and the new Jerusalem look like brothers.

isr-a-belyj-gorod.s: In Tel Aviv more than a thousand houses were built in a special style called “Bauhaus”. The houses are white and simple, with straight walls, round balconies and long windows. White reflects the sun, and the balconies make shade, so the rooms stay cooler when it is hot. These streets are called the White City. They are so special that a world organisation that protects the most precious places on Earth put them on a special list.
a: So planes can see them at night
Because there was no other paint

isr-a-karmelit.s: Haifa has an underground railway, and it is one of the shortest in the world. It is called the Carmelit. It has just one line, six stations and is about two kilometres long. But it is no ordinary underground: it goes up a hill, and the hill is steep. So the floor of the carriage is made in steps, so that passengers do not slide down. The trip from the bottom station to the top takes only a few minutes. The trains run under the ground, so outside you only see a little door.
a: The train goes up a steep hill

isr-a-zvyozdy-negeva.s: At night the Negev desert is very dark and quiet. There are few lights, so the sky sparkles as it never does in a city. There are so many stars that they melt into a pale path. That is the Milky Way. Near Ramon Crater there is even a special place where the lights are dimmed, so nothing disturbs the stars. People come with blankets, lie on the sand and look for shooting stars. And in the morning the desert wakes up pink.

isr-b-waze.s: Waze is a map app that tells a driver the way. It has a secret: the drivers help it. If there is a traffic jam or a hole in the road, someone presses a button, and everyone else finds out early and drives round it. The app was invented in Israel in the 2000s, and its sign is a smiling face. Later the big company Google bought it, and now people all over the world use it.

isr-b-pita.s: Pita is a round, flat bread baked in a very hot oven. It holds a little magic: when the dough gets hot, steam puffs it up like a balloon, and a hollow is left inside. The bread is cut open, and there is a pocket! People fill it with falafel (fried balls made of chickpeas), fresh cucumbers, tomatoes, salad and sauce. You hold this sandwich with both hands so nothing falls out, and eat it right in the street.

isr-b-purim.s: At Purim, everyone in Israel dresses up! In the streets you meet princesses, pirates, clowns, astronauts and even talking bananas. Children wear costumes to school, and the towns hold merry parades. At Purim people give friends and neighbours pretty baskets of sweets. They also bake three-cornered biscuits filled with poppy seeds or jam, called “Haman’s ears”. The festival is noisy, funny and kind.

isr-b-sea-turtles.s: In summer, sea turtles come ashore on the sandy beaches of Israel’s Mediterranean coast. At night a turtle digs a hole, lays about a hundred ball-shaped eggs and covers them with sand. Two months later the babies hatch, as small as your palm. They run to the water, following the light at the horizon. Volunteers help the baby turtles: they guard the nests and make sure the little ones do not get lost. You must never touch the nests. Let them grow!

isr-b-solar-heaters.s: If you look at Israeli towns from above, almost every roof has shiny flat panels and white tanks. These are solar water heaters. The sun warms the water in the panels all day long, and in the evening hot water comes out of the tap, with no gas and no electricity. Israel has lots of sun almost all year round, so most families have free hot water. It is a simple idea, and it helps families and nature.

isr-a-koshki.s: In Jerusalem you meet cats at every step. They lie on warm steps, doze on windowsills and walk proudly along walls. The people feed them and do not chase them away. The cats are fluffy, ginger, grey and spotted, and each one seems to have its own bit of street. If you sit quietly on a stone bench, you may see another tailed neighbour stroll past, looking as if he is the boss of the whole city.

jpn-a-shibuya.s: In Tokyo there is a crossing that people love to film. It is called Shibuya. When the light turns green, the cars stop on every side, and people step onto the road from everywhere at once: from the right, from the left and even across the middle! They walk towards each other, but nobody bumps into anybody. Hundreds of people cross each time, and sometimes, they say, even thousands. When the light turns red, it all starts again.
a: People cross the road in every direction at once
People cross the road in only one direction

jpn-a-fushimi.s: In Kyoto there is a shrine called Fushimi Inari. A path leads to it through thousands of bright red gates called torii. They stand so close together that they make a long red tunnel, and sunbeams slip through the gaps. Stone foxes sit all around. People believe the foxes are messengers of Inari, the goddess of rice. Many of the foxes hold a key to the rice store in their mouths, or so they say!
a: A key to the rice store

jpn-a-hanami.s: In spring the sakura blooms in Japan, and the flowers cover the branches so thickly that the tree looks like a pink cloud. People go to the parks, spread blankets on the grass and have a picnic right under the blossoming branches. This is called “hanami”, which means “looking at flowers”. Sakura blooms for only a short time, just a week or two, and then the petals fall like pink snow. So every day of the blossom is precious.

jpn-b-nos-zimorodka.s: The bullet train in Japan is called the Shinkansen. In the past, when a fast train flew into a tunnel, there was a loud bang at the other end. An engineer who loved watching birds thought of the kingfisher. This bird dives into water with hardly a splash. So the train was given a long nose like a kingfisher’s beak. With a nose like that, the train enters the tunnel quietly and smoothly.

jpn-b-himeji.s: Himeji Castle is called the White Heron. Its walls are covered with white plaster, and its curved roofs look like spread wings. It seems that a huge bird is standing on the hill, about to take off. The main tower was finished around the year 1609, so the castle is more than four hundred years old. It is on UNESCO’s World Heritage list, and visitors love to come here from all over the world.

jpn-c-snow-monkeys.s: In the mountains of Japan, in the Jigokudani valley, deep snow lies in winter. And in the warm water of a hot spring sit macaques! Only their little faces with red cheeks show above the water, and snowflakes sparkle on their fur. The macaques love to warm up, and the babies play nearby. They say the first little monkey climbed into the spring in the 1960s, and the others followed. Now they have their own pool.
a: In the warm water of a hot spring
In a house made of snow

jpn-c-nara-deer.s: In the park in the city of Nara, more than a thousand deer wander about, and nobody is afraid of them. They come up to people and ask for a snack. Special biscuits are sold for them, called “shika senbei”, made from rice bran. When a deer wants a biscuit, it often nods its head, as if it is bowing. Children bow back and hold out the treat on their open hand. People in Nara have believed for a very long time that the deer are messengers of the gods.
a: They nod their heads, as if bowing
They wag their tails like dogs

jpn-c-sapporo-snow.s: In the north of Japan, on the island of Hokkaido, there is a city called Sapporo. Every winter it holds a snow festival. Huge sculptures appear in the long park in the middle of the city: castles, animals and storybook heroes, as tall as houses! Everything is made of snow and ice. It began small: in 1950, some schoolchildren made six snow figures in the park. People liked them, and now the festival is known all over the world. In the evening, the sculptures are lit up.

jpn-d-koinobori.s: The fifth of May is Children’s Day in Japan. Above the houses, on tall poles, people hang koinobori: long windsocks shaped like carp. The wind fills them, and the fish seem to swim through the sky! A carp is stubborn and strong, and it can swim up a river against the current. So people in Japan wish their children to grow up brave and strong. Often one pole has several carp, big and small, like a whole family.

jpn-d-bento.s: Japanese children often take a bento to school: a lunch box with little sections. In one there is rice, in another some fish or a rolled omelette, in a third some vegetables. And the favourite is onigiri: a rice ball or triangle with a filling inside, often wrapped in a sheet of dried seaweed called nori. Sometimes mums arrange the food into little animal faces, so a child is happy to open the box.
a: A lunch box with several sections

jpn-a-skytree.s: In Tokyo stands a tower called the Tokyo Skytree. It is 634 metres tall, one of the tallest towers in the world! The number 634 was not chosen by chance: in Japanese, the numbers “mu-sa-shi” sound like “Musashi”, the old name of this land. From the top you can see the whole city, and on a clear day even faraway Mount Fuji. The lift whisks people up so fast that your ears probably pop.

jpn-a-tuna.s: Tokyo has a huge fish market called Toyosu. Long ago the market was in a place called Tsukiji, but in 2018 it moved to a new home. Very early, while it is still dark outside, there is an auction where big tunas are sold. One fish can be longer than a grown-up and heavier than several children! Visitors can watch from above, from a special corridor with windows, so they do not get in the way of the workers.

jpn-a-kinkaku.s: In Kyoto stands the Golden Pavilion, Kinkaku-ji. Its two top floors are covered with thin sheets of real gold! The pavilion stands by a pond, and in the still water you can see a second one, upside down. When the sun peeks out, it shines so brightly that your eyes tickle. Long ago it was the country home of a great ruler, and later it became a temple. People come from all over the world to see it.

jpn-a-bamboo.s: On the edge of Kyoto, in a place called Arashiyama, there is a bamboo grove. The bamboo stems are thick and very tall, much taller than a person. They stand so close together that walking along the path feels like walking down a green corridor. When the wind blows, the bamboo sways and rustles and softly knocks. People like this sound so much that the grove was put on the list of the “100 Soundscapes of Japan”.

jpn-a-fuji.s: Fuji is the highest mountain in Japan, 3,776 metres tall. It is a volcano, but it has been asleep for a long time: it last woke up more than three hundred years ago, in 1707. The top of the mountain is white even when it is still warm down below, because a snowy cap lies there for a long time. Fuji is so beautiful that Japanese people often draw it in paintings and postcards. You can usually climb it in summer, when the path is free of snow.
a: A sleeping volcano with a snowy cap
A huge rock on a beach

jpn-b-asimo.s: The robot ASIMO was invented by the Honda company. He is about as tall as a child, walks on two legs and can even run. ASIMO can climb stairs and pour a drink into a glass. He waves his hand as if saying hello. Engineers taught him to walk for many years, because standing steadily on two legs is very hard, especially for a robot. In 2022 ASIMO went into a well-earned retirement.

jpn-c-cat-island.s: Off the coast of Japan lies a tiny island called Aoshima. Very few people live there, mostly fishermen, but there are many more cats! People say the cats were brought there long ago to catch mice on the fishing boats. The cats stayed and had kittens. They lie on the quay, warm themselves in the sun and wait for the fishermen to come back with their catch. Visitors come to the island to meet them.
a: To catch mice on the boats

jpn-d-tanabata.s: On the seventh of July, Japanese people celebrate Tanabata. An old legend tells of two stars, Vega and Altair. A river of the sky, the Milky Way, keeps them apart, and they can meet only once a year. People write their wishes on colourful strips of paper and tie them to bamboo branches. The result is whole green trees hung with dreams, rustling softly in the wind. In some places the festival is held in August.

jpn-d-tea.s: Japan has a special tea ceremony, and it is never hurried. The tea master whisks green matcha powder with hot water, using a little bamboo whisk, until a soft foam rises. Before the tea, guests are given a small sweet, so that the tea tastes gentler. You hold the cup with two hands, and before drinking you turn it carefully. Every movement is slow and calm, like quiet music.

jpn-d-torii.s: Torii gates stand at the entrance to Japanese shrines. They are often bright red, with two posts and two crossbeams. They show that a special place begins behind them, and many people bow a little as they walk through. On the island of Miyajima, a huge gate stands right in the sea. When the tide is high, it looks as if the gate is floating on the water, and when the water goes out, you can walk to it.
a: The entrance to a special place, a shrine
The start of a football pitch

lis-bertrand.s: In Lisbon, in the Chiado area, there is a bookshop called Bertrand. It opened in 1732 and has sold books for almost three hundred years! The Guinness Book of Records named it the oldest working bookshop in the world. Inside there are several rooms, one after another, with shelves of books everywhere. When the shop opened, there was no electricity yet, and people read by candlelight.
a: It is the oldest in the world
It is the wettest in the world
It is the prickliest in the world
